item.title: Why "Green Prescriptions" Work
item.description:
Forest Bathing

Why "Green Prescriptions" Work

How other species can restore our mental health.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Green prescriptions offer a nature‑based alternative to traditional medicinal therapeutics.
  • Time in nature reduces stress, improves mood, and strengthens attention and creativity.
  • Building your own green prescription doesn’t require wilderness. Local green spaces work just as well.

We spend a lot of time trying to fix ourselves from the inside out. We tweak our mindset, optimize our productivity, refine our self‑care rituals. We read endless self-help books and follow threads about boundaries, attachment styles, and nervous system regulation.

But for all this effort, many of us feel more anxious, lonely, and disconnected than ever. What if one of the most powerful ways to improve our mental health isn’t in a book? What if it’s as easy as walking out your door?

Why "Green Prescriptions" Could Be a Mental-Health Gamechanger

Through my work as a behavioral ecologist, I’ve come to realize that by paying close attention to other species, I improve my own life, relationships, work, and sense of community. I’ve sat for hours with prairie dogs in the grasslands and lately gorillas in the forests of southwestern Uganda. I’ve spent countless mornings walking in my neighborhood watching the squirrels and birds start their day. And I spent 18 years with a cat who reorganized my entire schedule. Over and over, other species have been my best teachers in how to live, relate, build community, and stay present.

In my own work and in conversations with colleagues like primatologist Dr. Christine Webb, I’ve become increasingly interested in “green prescriptions,” which is essentially where traditional approaches don’t achieve the desired outcome and the final recommendation is to go outside. I would like to suggest we reverse the order.

A green prescription is a treatment plan that deliberately includes time in nature and contact with other living beings as part of mental and physical healthcare. In practice, that might mean being told to walk in a forest three times a week, spend time in a community garden, sit with birds in a city park, or engage with animals in ethical, non‑extractive ways.

Back in 2021, I interviewed psychiatrist Dr. Katherine Kennett on my podcast, "Wild Connection." A specialist in treating young people, Dr. Kennett advocates for a nature-based approach to mental health. Specifically, she works with her patients to develop and implement treatment plans that include incorporating more green space into their lives, developing sustainable interactions with nature, and getting involved in activities that preserve the natural environment. But the history of “green prescriptions” goes back much farther.

article continues after advertisement

History—and Research—Show That Green Prescriptions Work

Shinrin-yoku is a very old practice in Japan. Shinrin-yoku translates into “taking in the forest atmosphere” or “forest bathing,” and it involves immersing yourself in nature and engaging all of your senses.

Research out of Japan shows very clearly that exposure to forests reduces cortisol, lowers blood pressure and heart rate, and engages our calming parasympathetic nervous system, thus lowering our sympathetic fight or flight system. This is why, in the 1980s, the Japanese government began an earnest campaign advising people to engage in forest bathing.

The phrase "forest bathing" has become trendy, but it transcends a fad and is a viable clinical option. Instead of reaching for yet another medication to blunt a vague sense of dis‑ease, patients are encouraged to change the way they relate to the natural world. If you’re still skeptical, let’s turn to the research.

Studies of “greening” urban spaces similarly show significant reductions in stress and anxiety, lower rates of certain health problems, and even decreases in crime in neighborhoods that have more trees and accessible green areas. At the individual level, many people report feeling less lonely and more grounded when they regularly spend time in places where plants, animals, fungi, and other beings are visibly going about their lives.

From my perspective, these findings aren’t surprising. When I am with other species like prairie dogs, gorillas, ants, birds, or trees, I am fully present. You simply cannot pay attention to other beings and be checked‑out, scrolling on your phone, or obsessing over the latest conflict you're having with someone. Other species demand a kind of real‑time focus that pulls you out of your head and back into your body. Green prescriptions are a formal way of acknowledging something many of us already know intuitively: being in natural spaces is good for us.

How to Bring More Nature Into Your Own Life

Beyond just being good for us, implementing your own green prescriptions can impact many parts of your life. Regular time in nature can improve sleep quality, strengthen our immune function, and enhance attention and creativity. It can also shift how we show up in our relationships and workplaces, because spending time in green spaces—yes, even urban parks!—is soothing, which can make us less reactive and more aware of the fact that we are part of a larger living community, not the center of it.

article continues after advertisement

If you’re wondering where to start, you don’t need a cabin in the woods or a plane ticket. You can begin by creating your own simple green prescription:

  • Commit to a short daily “micro‑walk” outside, where your only job is to notice three living things and how they’re interacting with their environment.
  • Choose one nearby spot (e.g., a tree outside your office, a patch of grass by your building, a park bench) and visit it twice a week, paying attention to what other living creatures (beyond humans) are there.
  • Replace one indoor, screen‑based routine (like scrolling before bed) with a small, repeatable outdoor ritual, such as listening to birds at dusk or watching the way the light changes on a particular plant.

These may seem small or even silly at first, but over time you will notice how your attention changes, the details you start to see, or how you feel different during these activities. You might start even craving more of them!

For more tips, check out my course Reconnect with Nature and the companion workbook, Rooted in Nature.

item.title: Why Someone Else's Anxiety Makes Us Anxious
item.description:
Anxiety

Why Someone Else's Anxiety Makes Us Anxious

When we absorb other people’s anxiety and how therapy can help.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Another person’s anxiety can activate unconscious patterns rooted in early attachment dynamics.
  • Emotional absorption may reflect a past need to regulate others to feel safe in chaotic environments.
  • Our urge to soothe others may mask a deeper fear of helplessness and emotional disintegration.
  • Anxiety therapy helps increase emotional differentiation and tolerance of relational vulnerability.

Becoming anxious in response to another person’s anxiety is familiar for many people, including many of my patients. Whether it is the urgency in a friend’s voice, the distress of a romantic partner, or the unspokn tension in a colleague’s presence, we may find ourselves suddenly uneasy without an identifiable source within ourselves.

This experience is usually not only about being empathic, emotionally attuned, or “sensitive.” It is often useful to consider that deeper and more complex dynamics are involved. What might be happening within ourselves that makes us more vulnerable to taking in other people's anxiety as if it was ours? Anxiety is not merely a surface-level emotion but a form of internal communication and, for many people, often an unconscious enactment of early relational dynamics in our life. This post explores why someone else’s anxiety can so readily trigger our own and how anxiety therapy can help.

Anxiety Is More Than a Feeling

Anxiety is a natural human emotion. It is not only not "bad" in itself, but it's useful and necessary at times. It can also be a very disturbing and disruptive experience. While many people have the understandable wish to make it go away, understanding it more deeply can be important because it might be connected with different parts of who we are. Anxiety, in that way, can be seen less as just a symptom to be eliminated and more as a signal that something intolerable or overwhelming is threatening to emerge from within, whether it is an internal conflict or a perceived threat. This distress is often connected to different types of fear, including the fear of being judged, abandoned, retraumatized, or psychologically annihilated.

When one is in the presence of another’s anxiety, it is not merely an observation of their distress. The anxious person, often unknowingly, may externalize and displace internal tension into what has been called “the relational field,” the co-created space that exists between two people in all human interactions. The recipient, in turn, may unconsciously absorb or be drawn into this distress, not out of conscious choice, but because something deep in their mind is being activated.

Early Relationships and the Drive to Co-Regulate

Much of our vulnerability to others’ emotional states is shaped by early developmental experiences. Infant researchers have, for the last few decades, uncovered and explored the co-regulatory processes that start from birth with our caregivers. These processes are intricate, continuous, and often out of our awareness. When things go well enough, children can develop not only the capacity to recognize and tolerate their internal emotional states, but also the trust that the other person will be able to regulate their own emotions as well.

article continues after advertisement

In contrast, in families where caregivers were inconsistent, emotionally fragile, or overwhelmed, the child may have learned that their own stability depended on the regulation of those around them. Such children often assume the role of emotional caretaker, suppressing their needs, heightening their sensitivity, and organizing their behavior around the perceived emotional climate of the household.

Similarly, growing up in a family with blurry boundaries between self and other, marked by patterns of enmeshment and undifferentiation, might lead the child to feel that their sense of identity is contingent on the needs or feelings of others. In such cases, another person’s anxiety does not feel external. The other’s emotional state feels indistinguishable from our own, leading to a kind of emotional contagion that is difficult to parse or resist.

These early adaptations form relational templates and attachment patterns that persist into adulthood. In that context, the presence of anxiety in another might be unconsciously registered as a potential threat or elicit roles we have played in earlier relationships. When someone close to us becomes anxious, we may reflexively enter a state of internal alert. Even if we are not directly in danger, our old templates might get activated: “I need you to be okay so that I can be okay.”

Sometimes this template may be expressed in rescuing, caretaking, or soothing behaviors towards the other. However, it can also be experienced through the internalization of their emotional state. By making their anxiety ours, we unconsciously wish that we might make it go away for them. Absorbing the other person’s anxiety might be, we hope, a way to make our environment calmer and safer. These dynamics are often outside of conscious awareness and can lead to a profound and automatic internal reaction, particularly in close relationships. Moreover, they can become part of how we organize our whole personality.

Anxiety therapy informed by psychodynamic principles attends to these relational blueprints. It does not simply seek to reduce symptoms, but rather to explore the internal narratives and emotional roles that continue to shape how one experiences anxiety in relation to others.

The Intolerance of Helplessness

article continues after advertisement

Being around someone else’s anxiety, particularly a person close to us, can lead us to feel helpless. Observing or being confronted with another’s anxiety often evokes a sense of urgency or compulsion to act. The impulse to soothe, advise, or intervene is not only a sign of care, but it can also be a way to mitigate the intolerable feeling of powerlessness.

For many individuals, their (in)capacity to tolerate helplessness is linked to early experiences of emotional abandonment, inconsistency, or chaos. When one could not control the environment or our caregivers’ behaviors or affective states, helplessness became associated with danger, isolation, or shame. We may have even felt responsible or blamed ourselves for other people’s anxiety and distress, as a way to gain some sense of power and control over an otherwise scary or painful experience.

Our anxiety in response to someone else’s operates not only as a response to the other person’s state, but as a defense against the internal vulnerability that helplessness creates. The need to do something becomes a way to disavow the reality that we may, in fact, not be able to alter another person’s emotional condition.

A central aim of anxiety therapy in such cases is to help the individual recognize and tolerate these moments of helplessness without collapsing into anxiety or reactive behavior. This involves developing the capacity to observe one’s own internal responses with curiosity rather than urgency.

How Can Anxiety Therapy Help?

Psychoanalytic psychotherapy does not pathologize anxiety, nor does it aim simply to eliminate it. Instead, it treats anxiety as a meaningful expression of unconscious conflicts, fears, and relational history. By exploring the ways in which another person’s anxiety resonates with one’s internal world, therapy can start creating the conditions for greater differentiation, self-possession, and emotional clarity.

article continues after advertisement

Over time, people can come to recognize their own patterns of emotional absorption and regulation, develop an increased capacity for emotional differentiation, and tolerate the inevitable moments of helplessness that human relationships entail. This is what anxiety therapy can offer: not quick fixes, but a deeper kind of change — one where we become more able to hold the complexity of feeling without being consumed by it, or rushing to solve or avoid.

item.title: At This Age, "No" Is a Complete Sentence
item.description:
Aging

At This Age, "No" Is a Complete Sentence

Personal Perspective: FOMO doesn't check the age on your ID.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • FOMO may be telling you something true: that you've gotten too isolated or stopped taking risks.
  • Is your fear actually pointing you toward something you want? Or is it just the noise of comparison?
  • By now we can tell the difference between a life that needs more and a life that simply needs less clutter.

No single entity illustrates life's pathways in later life better than Hollywood. Remember The Shawshank Redemption? Two old men are both released after decades behind bars.

Brooks, who had spent so long institutionalized that the outside world no longer made sense to him, carved, "Brooks was here" into a rafter and then just gave up. He had no desire to adapt to what the world had become.

Then there's Red, who had just as many years in, and who carved, "Red was here" in the same rafter — and then hopped a bus to Mexico to find his friend on a beach: same room, same rafter, and a completely different relationship with the time they had left.

"Get busy livin' or get busy dyin'." That line has stayed with me for decades, because it captures something I think about a lot when it comes to aging and FOMO — the Fear of Missing Out.

While we may have borrowed the word from millennials, make no mistake: FOMO doesn't check the age on your ID. It's the persistent anxiety that others are having experiences you're not, and that your life is somehow diminished for it. Young or old, many of us scroll Instagram at midnight (waiting for the NYTimes games to refresh), paralyzed by someone else's vacation photos and life transformations. But we older adults experience FOMO along the same spectrum as younger generations. At our age, it just gets a tad more ridiculous.

I'll cover the three versions worth naming, each with its own personality. There's the social version: the feeling that life is happening somewhere without you. It's like that scene from Trading Places, where once-snooty Dan Aykroyd watches his former associates through a restaurant window while he's stuck outside in the rain in a sopping Santa suit.

The existential version deals a reckoning with time — that quiet dread that the clock is running and the experiences you haven't had yet may never happen. It's heavier than regular FOMO, more honest, and its own kind of uncomfortable.

And then there's the wellness version, which is its own circus: GLP-1s, peptides, hormone debates, the supplement your friend swears changed her life, or the longevity protocol your other friend found on a podcast. New stuff flashes by weekly. While most of it is noise, there is still that feeling that everyone else has cracked the code and you missed getting the memo.

In reasonable doses, however, FOMO is actually motivating. It's what gets you to say yes to the trip you'd otherwise talk yourself out of, sign up for a class, take a call, or try a thing. The FOMO that propels you toward something is useful. The one that leaves you scrolling someone else's highlight reel, less so.

article continues after advertisement

How about those Book Club movies, where four perfectly competent older adults needed a certain scandalous novel to remind them they weren't done wanting things? That's FOMO doing its job. The kind that says, "Pay attention. There's still time."

The counterweight to FOMO that deserves far more airtime, especially for women our age, however, is JOMO. The Joy of Missing Out. Research suggests that older adults report significantly higher levels of JOMO than younger people. We gain the ability to genuinely enjoy saying no — to the obligation, the trip we never really wanted to take, or the dinner party we knew would have us spending three hours pretending to care about someone's kitchen renovation. Just when you think you've become antisocial, you realize you've developed a hard-won, deeply satisfying skill and offer no apologies whatsoever.

My mentor Nora Ephron understood this. She wrote and talked often about the importance of knowing when to leave the party. Studies show that embracing intentional opting-out is associated with higher life satisfaction and better well-being. Make no mistake about it, however: JOMO and FOMO can coexist. You can fear missing out and also deeply enjoy staying home in your grubbies watching Meryl Streep in Bridges of Madison County.

Before you think you have to shake off FOMO, consider that it may be telling you something true: that you've gotten too isolated, that you've stopped taking risks, that what you're calling "preference" is actually just fear of looking frumpy wearing flat shoes — and you've been in heels most of your life.

So is your fear actually pointing you toward something you want? Or is it just the noise of comparison, insisting your life should look like someone else's?

That scene in When Harry Met Sally where Sally orders everything on the side says it all. Harry sits transfixed, eyes wide in disbelief. Even at her young age (while annoying to those around her), Sally figured out what she actually wanted and stopped pretending otherwise. That's not giving up. We writers call it editing. And editing, as any of us will tell you, is where the real work happens.

At this point in life, we have enough data on ourselves to tell the difference between a life that needs more in it and a life that simply needs less clutter. The trick is staying honest about which is which — and then ordering exactly what you want, no substitutions. In most cases, you're not missing a thing.
